title: Dancing Queens: The Pawn Endings
summary: After the queens are exchanged, combine a king march toward the outside pawn with timely advances of your own passer.

nodes.question: Which task should the king handle first?
nodes.explanation: Begin in the five-piece pawn ending with White Kd6 and c4 against Kb1, c5 and h6. White can remove c5 immediately, then use both the king and passed pawn.

nodes.question: What changes if the king is still on e7?
nodes.explanation: This separate five-piece source ending has White Ke7 instead of Kd6. The exact position is losing for White; the larger queen sequences leading to these endings are not encoded.

branches.title: Capture c5, stop the outside pawn, then promote
commentary: Begin in the five-piece pawn ending with White Kd6 and c4 against Kb1, c5 and h6. White can remove c5 immediately, then use both the king and passed pawn.
Kxc5 removes the central pawn and turns c4 into a passed pawn. This capture is essential.
h5 starts the outside-pawn race, trying to divert the white king.
Kd4 heads toward the kingside while keeping the c-pawn available to advance.
h4 continues the distraction. White must use the king and pawn together.
Ke3 approaches the h-file via f3 and g2.
Kc2 chases the c-pawn. This is an independently selected representative reply within the source’s pawn-race idea.
c5 advances before the black king can arrive in time to stop it.
Kc3 continues the chase from behind.
c6 keeps the passer ahead of the king while White’s king handles h3/h2.
h3 threatens to create a second queen quickly.
Kf3 gets within reach of the promotion route.
h2 moves one square from promotion.
Kg2 controls h1. Promotion can now be met by capture.
h1=Q+ promotes with check in this independent representative continuation. The new queen is not safe.
Kxh1 removes the outside pawn’s promotion. White’s c6 pawn remains far enough ahead of the black king.
Kd4 continues toward c6, but the pawn can move again.
c7 leaves only one move to promotion.
Kd5 is a representative legal chase that still arrives too late.
c8=Q promotes. The exact queen-versus-king position is a White win.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: c8=Q promotes. The exact queen-versus-king position is a White win.

branches.title: The earlier exchange leaves the king too far away
commentary: This comparison starts from the separately pictured ending with Ke7, not from an assumed continuous move list between the queen sequences. The replies are independently selected.
Kf6 heads toward the outside pawn, but White has not removed c5.
h5 creates the distraction while the black king approaches c4.
Kg5 continues toward the h-pawn.
Ka2 brings Black’s king closer to the c-pawn.
Kxh5 removes the distraction, but the white king is now far from the queenside.
Kb3 attacks c4 and threatens to leave Black with the only passed pawn.
Kg4 starts back across the board too late in this selected continuation.
Kxc4 removes White’s pawn. The exact king-and-c-pawn ending is winning for Black.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Kxc4 removes White’s pawn. The exact king-and-c-pawn ending is winning for Black.

branches.title: March away before taking c5
commentary: Begin in the five-piece pawn ending with White Kd6 and c4 against Kb1, c5 and h6. White can remove c5 immediately, then use both the king and passed pawn.
Kd5 abandons the immediate capture on c5 and throws away the win. The exact resulting position is losing for White with best play; capturing c5 was the urgent first task.

exercises.prompt: Why combine king movement with pawn advances?
exercises.answer: The king must stop the h-pawn while c5/c6 keep the other passer beyond the black king’s reach. Capturing c5 first creates that opportunity.

exercises.prompt: Why is capturing the outside pawn alone insufficient?
exercises.answer: If White’s king spends its time on the h-file while c5 remains, Black can collect c4 and retain the only passed pawn.

startContext: This study checks the two five-piece pawn endings shown at 157 seconds (Kd6, winning) and 33 seconds (Ke7, losing). The earlier nine-piece queen dances and the source’s Kd6 tempo claim remain source context, outside this exact reconstruction. Encoded pawn-race continuations use explicitly independent representative replies from those pictured endings.
